exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Paraboloid

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(y, z) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: y, \: z \big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(y, z)$ above parametrizes the hyperbolic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $2x=3y^2-4z^2.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
Solving our equation for $x,$ we obtain

\[ 2x=3y^2-4z^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=\dfrac32y^2-2z^2. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(y, z) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \Big\langle {\color{blue}\dfrac32y^2-2z^2}, \: y, \: z \Big\rangle \end{align*}

where $y \in (-\infty,\infty)$ and $z \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}\dfrac32y^2-2z^2}.$

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(x, z) = \Big\langle x, \: \text{_____}, \: z \Big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(x, z)$ above parametrizes the hyperbolic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $2y=8z^2-x^2.$ What is the second component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
Solving our equation for $y,$ we obtain

\[ 2y=8z^2-x^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y=4z^2-\dfrac{x^2}{2}. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(x, z) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \Big\langle x, \: {\color{blue}4z^2-\dfrac{x^2}{2}}, \: z \Big\rangle \end{align*}

where $x \in (-\infty,\infty)$ and $z \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the second component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}4z^2-\dfrac{x^2}{2}}.$

example.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Paraboloid

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(x, y) = \big\langle x, \: y, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(x, y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\dfrac{z}{2}=3x^2+4y^2.$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
Solving our equation for $z,$ we obtain

\[ \dfrac{z}{2}=3x^2+4y^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad z=6x^2+8y^2. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(x, y) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle {x, \: y, \:\color{blue}6x^2+8y^2} \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $x \in (-\infty,\infty)$ and $y \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}6x^2+8y^2}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Polar Parametrization of a Paraboloid

question.text:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(r,\theta),$ given by

\[ \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) = \big\langle r^2, \:\text{_____}, \: 4 r \sin\theta \big\rangle \]

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as
\[ x=\dfrac{y^2}{9}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}. \] By first considering the transformations \[ x = Z, \qquad y = 3X, \qquad z = 4Y \]

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $\mathbf{f}.$
question.explanation:
First, substituting the transformations

\[ x = Z, \qquad y = 3X, \qquad z = 4Y \]

into our equation, we get

\[ Z = X^2 + Y^2. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = z. \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} Z &= X^2+Y^2 \\[5pt] Z &= (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2 \\[5pt] Z &= r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta) \\[5pt] Z &= r^2. \end{align*}

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(r, \theta) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[5pt] &= \langle Z,3X,4Y \rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle Z, \:3 r \cos\theta, \: 4 r \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle r^2, \: {\color{blue}3 r \cos\theta}, \: {4 r \sin\theta} \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $r \in [0,\infty)$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi).$

Therefore, the second component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} 3 r \cos\theta}.$

example.title: Finding a Polar Parametrization of a Paraboloid

question.text:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(r,\theta),$ given by

\[ \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) = \big\langle \text{_____} , \: r \sin\theta, \: r^2 \big\rangle \]

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as \[ z=\dfrac{x^2}{9}+y^2. \] By first considering the transformations \[ x =3X, \qquad y = Y, \qquad z = Z \]

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the first component of $\mathbf{f}.$
question.explanation:
First, substituting the transformations

\[ x = 3X, \qquad y = Y, \qquad z = Z \]

into our equation, we get

\[ Z = X^2 + Y^2. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = z. \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} Z &= X^2+Y^2 \\[5pt] Z &= (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2 \\[5pt] Z &= r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta) \\[5pt] Z &= r^2. \end{align*}

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(r, \theta) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[5pt] &= \langle 3X,Y,Z \rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle 3r \cos\theta, \: r \sin\theta, \: Z \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle {\color{blue}3r \cos\theta}, \: r \sin\theta, \: r^2 \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $r \in [0,\infty)$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} 3r \cos\theta}.$

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as
\[ y=\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}. \] By first considering the transformations \[ x = 2Y, \qquad y = Z, \qquad z = 4X \]

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the third component of $\mathbf{f}.$
question.explanation:
First, substituting the transformations

\[ x = 2Y, \qquad y = Z, \qquad z = 4X \]

into our equation, we get

\[ Z = X^2 + Y^2. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = z. \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} Z &= X^2+Y^2 \\[5pt] Z &= (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2 \\[5pt] Z &= r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta) \\[5pt] Z &= r^2. \end{align*}

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Hyperboloid of One Sheet

question.text:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi),$ given by

\[ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \text{_____}, 5\cosh\phi\sin\theta, \: 7\cosh\phi\cos\theta \big\rangle \]

parametrizes the hyperboloid of one sheet defined in Cartesian coordinates as

\[ -x^2+\dfrac{y^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{49}=1. \]

By first considering the transformations \[ x = Z, \qquad y = 5Y, \qquad z = 7X \]

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the first component of $\mathbf{f}.$

Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola $r^2-Z^2 = k^2$ can be parametrized as $\langle r, Z\rangle = \langle k\cosh\phi, k\sinh \phi\rangle $ for $\phi\in \mathbb R.$
question.explanation:
First, substituting the transformations

\[ x = Z, \qquad y = 5Y, \qquad z = 7X \]

into our equation, we get

\[ X^2 + Y^2 - Z^2 = 1. \]

If $(r, \theta, Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = Z. \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} X^2+Y^2-Z^2 &= 1 \\[3pt] (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2-Z^2 &= 1 \\[3pt] r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta)-Z^2 &= 1 \\[3pt] r^2 - Z^2 &= 1. \end{align*}

Here, the hyperbola $r^2 - Z^2 = 1$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $Z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta$ with the positive $X$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

\[ \langle r, Z \rangle = \langle \cosh{\phi}, \: \sinh{\phi} \rangle, \qquad \phi \in \mathbb R. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle Z,5Y,7X \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle Z, \: 5r \sin\theta, \: 7r\cos\theta \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \sinh\phi, \: 5(\cosh{\phi})\sin\theta, \: 7(\cosh{\phi})\cos\theta \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle {\color{blue}\sinh{\phi}} , \: 5\cosh\phi\sin\theta, \: 7\cosh{\phi} \cos\theta \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in \mathbb R.$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}\sinh{\phi} }.$

example.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Hyperboloid of One Sheet

question.text:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi),$ given by

\[ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle 5 \cosh{\phi} \cos\theta, \: 5 \cosh{\phi} \sin\theta, \: \text{_______} \big\rangle \]

parametrizes the hyperboloid of one sheet defined in Cartesian coordinates as $x^2+y^2-z^2=25.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the third component of $\mathbf{f}.$

Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola $r^2-z^2 = k^2$ can be parametrized as $\langle r, z\rangle = \langle k\cosh\phi, k\sinh \phi\rangle $ for $\phi\in \mathbb R.$
question.explanation:
If $(r, y, \theta)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z . \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} x^2+y^2-z^2 &= 25 \\[3pt] (r\cos\theta)^2+ (r\sin\theta)^2-z^2 &= 25 \\[3pt] r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta)-z^2 &=25 \\[3pt] r^2 - z^2 &= 25. \end{align*}

Here, the hyperbola $r^2 - z^2 = 25$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

\[ \langle r, z \rangle = \langle 5 \cosh{\phi}, \: 5 \sinh{\phi} \rangle, \qquad \phi \in \mathbb R. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle r \cos\theta, \: r \sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle (5 \cosh{\phi}) \cos\theta, \: (5\cosh{\phi}) \sin\theta , \: 5\sinh{\phi}\big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 5 \cosh{\phi} \cos\theta, \: 5\cosh{\phi} \sin\theta , \: {\color{blue}5\sinh{\phi}} \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in \mathbb R.$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}5\sinh{\phi}}.$

question.text:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi),$ given by

\[ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi} \cos\theta, \:\sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi}\sin\theta , \: \text{_____}\big\rangle \]

parametrizes the hyperboloid of one sheet defined in Cartesian coordinates as $x^2+y^2-z^2=2.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the third component of $\mathbf{f}.$

question.explanation:
If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

Substituting this into our equation, we get

\begin{align*} x^2+y^2-z^2 &= 2 \\[3pt] (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2-z^2 &= 2\\[3pt] r^2(\cos^2 \theta+\sin^2 \theta)-z^2 &= 2 \\[3pt] r^2 - z^2 &= 2. \end{align*}

Here, the hyperbola $r^2 - z^2 = 2$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

\[ \langle r, z \rangle = \langle \sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi}, \: \sqrt{2}\sinh{\phi} \rangle, \qquad \phi \in \mathbb R. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle r \cos\theta, \: r \sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle (\sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi}) \cos\theta, \: (\sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi}) \sin\theta, \: \sqrt{2}\sinh{\phi} \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi} \cos\theta, \: \sqrt{2}\cosh{\phi} \sin\theta, \: {\color{blue}\sqrt{2}\sinh{\phi}} \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in \mathbb R.$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}\sqrt{2}\sinh{\phi}}.$
